title: Jewish Heirs and Consignors Settle Claim Over $180 Million van Gogh Ahead of Sale
summary: Already the top lot of the season, the van Gogh became the center of controversy after a claim surfaced that it was sold under Nazi-era duress in the 1930s.

The shadow has finally cleared over a $180 million painting by Vincent van Gogh.


On Tuesday — just a day before the painting’s sale at Sotheby’s — the auction house said a settlement had been reached between its current owners and Jewish heirs of a previous owner. The[heirs had asked last week to stop the sale](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/arts/design/van-gogh-sale-sothebys.html) , claiming the work was sold in the 1930s by their ancestor under the duress of Nazi-era persecution.


Tuesday’s agreement, reached after tense negotiations, allows for the sale of the painting, “Châtaigniers en Fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees).” According to participants, the negotiations stretched from Monday morning into the early hours of Tuesday morning.


The auction is scheduled for Wednesday evening. A Sotheby’s news release gave no details of the settlement.


“In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement,” Sotheby’s said, adding that the company was “pleased to have helped facilitate this outcome and to see the matter resolved ahead of the sale.”


The Blaquier-Arrieta family, which bought the Van Gogh painting in 1975 and is selling it


as part of a trove assembled with their Argentine sugar fortune, said they had reached an amicable solution. “We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible,” the family said in a statement.


The heirs of the artwork’s previous owner, the German Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer, also praised the deal. In a statement, they said the negotiation would “make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era.”
